solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Who went to the land of Nod hugging fit old man?

indicators.note: to hug something is to wrap your arms around it, so one word sits inside the other

parts.words: Who went to the land of Nod
parts.note: Genesis says Cain went out and dwelt in the land of Nod after killing Abel
fit as an adjective: suitable

explanation.surface: A biblical exile embracing an elderly father who is in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' looks like the one being hugged; it is the definition, informal for a boss or a ship's commander.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors and crews have long called their skipper 'the old man', a slang name for the commander.

clue.text: Bluebottles finishing off shoe brush

parts.note: bluebottle is old slang for a policeman, from the blue uniform

indicators.note: the finishing part of a word is its end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Flies finishing off a shoe brush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bluebottles' looks like flies; it is slang for police. 'Brush' is not the tool but brushwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Brush means brushwood or scrubby undergrowth, and a copse is a small thicket of trees and bushes.

clue.text: Carefully check a resort, as was

parts.note: per means a or each, as in 'ten pounds per head'
use once meant to resort to or frequent a place; 'as was' marks the old sense

explanation.surface: Inspect a holiday resort as it used to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday spot; it is the verb for going to habitually.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse a document is to read through it carefully, examining it in detail.

clue.text: Greek hymns broadcast before bearing up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
A stands for ante, Latin for before
port means bearing or deportment, how someone carries themselves

explanation.surface: Greek hymns are aired before someone's composure rises.
explanation.walkthrough: AIR, A and PORT are joined and then the whole string is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Troparia, plural of troparion, are short hymns or stanzas sung in the Greek Orthodox liturgy.

clue.text: Fête in need of opening — take something to clear the air

indicators.note: a word that needs its opening has lost it, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: to fête someone is to lionize them, treat them as a celebrity
R stands for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A garden fête that needs opening, with a request to take an air freshener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fête' looks like a summer fair; it is the verb meaning to celebrate a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An ionizer is a device that charges particles in the air to remove dust and pollen, purifying it.

clue.text: Tree's preposterous synonym so far taken up

indicators.note: preposterous literally means before-behind, so the word is put back to front
in a down clue, taken up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: SYN is the dictionary abbreviation for synonym, here turned round
as can mean so far, as in 'as far as it goes', here turned round

explanation.surface: A tree is an absurd synonym that has been adopted so far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preposterous' is used in its Latin sense of back to front. SYN reversed, then AS reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nyssa is the tupelo genus, a group of trees found in North America and Asia.

clue.text: Daughter's missing German and oddly the Scots adventures

indicators.note: done oddly means done in a strange, jumbled way, so the following short word's letters are shuffled
something missing is absent, so these letters are taken out of the longer word

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored
G is the standard abbreviation for German
taken as written

explanation.surface: A daughter misses a German companion and the strange Scottish escapades.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove G and a jumbled THE (as the run GHTE) from DAUGHTERS. The blog's note says D, but it is G that goes.
explanation.definitionFit: DAUR is the Scots form of dare, and to adventure is to venture or dare, so daurs means ventures in Scots.

clue.text: Rab C's more sober, otherwise cured of being held

indicators.note: something being held is gripped inside, so the short word goes within the rest
otherwise means in another way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
o' is a shortened form of of

explanation.surface: Rab C. Nesbitt being more sober, or else cured of being locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Rab C. Nesbitt is a Glaswegian TV character, so the definition asks for a Scots word. O goes in and the letters of CURED are rearranged around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Douce is Scots for sober or sedate, and doucer is its comparative, more sober.

clue.text: Wooden group wrapped up in soul music

indicators.note: something wrapped up in a phrase is enclosed by it, so the answer sits inside these words

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A band of wooden performers absorbed in soul music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wooden group' sounds like a stiff band; it is a group of trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulmus is the botanical genus of elms, a group of trees and so a woody group.

clue.text: Driving mist engulfing Scots isle, ultimately one gets a ticket for later

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up, so the island word goes inside the mist word

parts.note: rack is wind-driven cloud or mist
inch is the Scots word for a small island

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Swirling mist around a Scottish island ends with someone getting a deferred ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: Rack is an old word for wind-driven cloud, and an inch is a small Scottish island, as in Inchcolm.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain check was a ticket for a later game when rain stopped play, now any promise to take up an offer later.

clue.text: Letters dealt out decisive blow

indicators.note: cards dealt out are scattered from the pack, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Letters handed out struck a decisive blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A settler is a knockout punch or decisive argument, something that settles the matter.

clue.text: Public in Oxford Uni here! I'm done, another may go

parts.note: overt means open, done in public

indicators.note: a word placed in another sits inside it, here between the two letters for the university

parts.note: abbreviation of Oxford University
an informal call answering a roll-call, like 'present!'

explanation.surface: An exclamation about something being public at Oxford University.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here!' looks like part of the surface's exclamation; it is the roll-call reply 'Yo!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the radio or relay handover: the speaker has finished and passes the turn to the next person.

clue.text: Standard Old Latin is spoken

parts.note: par is the standard or norm
O is the abbreviation for old
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A remark that the standard form of Old Latin is the spoken one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Latin' looks like one phrase, but it supplies two separate abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Parol is a legal word for oral, given by word of mouth rather than in writing.

clue.text: Boat from Bremen with bow

parts.note: short for submarine
mit is German for with, and Bremen is a German city

explanation.surface: A vessel out of the German port of Bremen with a bow at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' looks like the front of the boat; it is the verb meaning to give way. 'From Bremen' flags a German word.
explanation.definitionFit: To bow to someone is to yield or defer to them, which is what submitting means.

clue.text: Ban relied on shifting queue of poor

indicators.note: something shifting keeps moving position, so the letters change places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A prohibition that depended on moving the line of needy people along.
explanation.definitionFit: A bread line is a queue of poor people waiting for free food handed out by charity.

clue.text: Take off slight peer

parts.note: to dis is slang for to slight or insult
a count is a nobleman, a peer

explanation.surface: Remove a minor nobleman from consideration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' suggests looking closely; here it is a titled noble.
explanation.definitionFit: To discount a price is to take an amount off it, a straightforward synonym for deducting.

clue.text: Phoney OT book, in short, about son lying in grass

indicators.note: about means around, so the short book name wraps the rest

parts.note: Ezra, an Old Testament book, cut down to its abbreviation

indicators.note: something lying in a place is inside it, so the single letter goes within the informer word

parts.note: to grass or rat is to inform on someone
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A fake abbreviated Bible book about a boy lying in the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like a lawn; it is British slang for informing on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz describes an inferior substitute or imitation, so it means fake or phoney.

clue.text: Miss helping in court — enjoy oneself finally visiting Ireland

parts.note: to ball is slang for having a great time, as in having a ball

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
IRL is the international code for Ireland

explanation.surface: A young woman assisting at a court case has fun on a trip to Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court; it is a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball-girl is a girl, a miss, who retrieves balls for the players during a tennis match.

clue.text: Small bank knocked back old companions

indicators.note: knocked back means pushed backwards, so the letters are read from right to left

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a reef is a ridge or bank just below the sea surface

explanation.surface: A little bank turned down some former friends.
explanation.walkthrough: S plus REEF, all read backwards. FEER is an old spelling of fere.
explanation.definitionFit: Fere or feer is an archaic word for a companion or mate, so the plural means old companions.

clue.text: Jack on ship who hoisted "England expects" etc

parts.note: a jack is a flag flown at a ship's bow
to man a ship is to crew it

explanation.surface: A sailor named Jack aboard the ship that raised Nelson's famous signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'England expects that every man will do his duty' was Nelson's flag signal at Trafalgar. 'Jack' looks like a sailor; it is a flag.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagman is someone who signals with flags, as the signal officer did when running up Nelson's message.

clue.text: English with a passé dog could be a pain

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written
rache is an obsolete word for a hunting dog that hunts by scent

explanation.surface: An English owner with an old-fashioned dog could find it a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passé' tells you the dog word is archaic: a rache was a scenting hound.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is one particular kind of pain, so 'a pain' gives it by example; it is also slang for nagging.

clue.text: Stiff singer usually seen dressed up

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unbending, refusing to change
second meaning: the 1980s pop star famous for dandy highwayman and pirate costumes

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is the stage name of the singer, read as two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means unyielding and inflexible, while Adam Ant is the flamboyantly costumed British new-wave singer.

clue.text: Line by señora, say, cutting special cord

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for line

indicators.note: cutting something out removes it, so the abbreviation is taken away from the nationality word

parts.note: a señora is an example of a Spanish woman, so 'say' signals a definition by example
SP is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A line near a Spanish lady slicing through a particular cord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' looks like it is cutting the cord; it means SP is cut out of SPANIARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A laniard, usually spelt lanyard, is a short rope or cord, such as one worn round the neck.

clue.text: Go for mug with trouble

parts.note: a mug is a fool, an ass
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Attack a fool who has been causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mug' looks like a cup or a face; it is a gullible person.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail someone is to attack them, and 'go for' is the informal phrase for attacking.

clue.text: Adapt that by which 'ighwayman 'anged

parts.note: a halter is a hangman's noose, and the dropped aitches tell you to drop the H too

explanation.surface: A Cockney-voiced line about how a highwayman met the noose.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing H in 'ighwayman and 'anged is the deletion signal: HALTER loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To alter something is to change or modify it, a plain synonym for adapting it.

clue.text: Container in Cadiz can just about open

indicators.note: just about means nearly, so the word is not quite complete and loses its last letter

parts.note: a can is a tin
ajar means slightly open

explanation.surface: A container in a Spanish port city that a can can just about open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Cadiz' tells you the word is Spanish. AJAR loses its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinaja is a large earthenware jar used in Spain for storing wine or oil.

clue.text: Food packaging beginning to attract seabird

indicators.note: packaging wraps around its contents, so the food word surrounds the letter

parts.note: chow is slang for food

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Food wrapping that starts to draw in a seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: The cahow is the Bermuda petrel, a rare seabird once thought extinct.

clue.text: Old muffle is supple I conceded

indicators.note: something conceded is given up, so this letter is surrendered from the word

parts.note: mobile means moving easily, supple
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old scarf is flexible, I admitted.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is archaic: Hamlet's 'mobled queen' is a muffled one.
explanation.definitionFit: To moble is an old verb meaning to wrap or muffle up the head, as in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Whole and stiff fish

parts.note: the whole is all of it
both are slang for kill: to stiff or ice someone

explanation.surface: An entire, rigid fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like an adjective for the fish; it is a slang verb meaning to murder, like ice.
explanation.definitionFit: The allice, or allis shad, is a European fish of the herring family.

clue.text: Bore to go along with putting up one on state benefit

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a letter up moves it higher, so it is placed at the top of the word

parts.note: E is the lowest social grade, which includes people living on state benefits
to go along with is to agree; one of its two final E's is the letter that gets moved

explanation.surface: A tiresome person who accepts putting up a claimant.
explanation.walkthrough: AGREE has one E moved up to the top: in a down clue, 'putting up' means moving it higher. 'Bore' is the tidal wave, not a dull person.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagre is a tidal bore, a wave surging up a river estuary such as the Trent.

clue.text: Quondam rollicking self-driving shriek kid's kept in

indicators.note: something kept in a place is held inside it, so the boy word goes within the shriek

parts.note: 'Go me!' is a cry urging yourself on
a kid is a lad, with the 's kept

explanation.surface: A once-merry self-driving car whose scream is heard by a child inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-driving' suggests a car; it means cheering yourself on, the shriek 'Go me!'. LADS goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladsome is an archaic word for cheerful or joyous, so 'quondam' (former) marks it as old.

clue.text: Niche boozer that bloke turned over

indicators.note: something turned over is flipped, so the joined words are read backwards

parts.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub or bar
the pronoun for that man

explanation.surface: A niche pub whose regular got overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: BAR plus HIM, all reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A mihrab is the niche in a mosque wall that shows worshippers the direction of Mecca.

clue.text: Head of state entertaining American ass

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them in, so one letter is held inside the ruler

parts.note: a monarch heads the state
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A monarch hosts a foolish American visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ass' looks like an insult for the American; it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The kiang is a wild ass native to the Tibetan plateau.

clue.text: It's airtight and helps keep dry judge in rear, in disarray

parts.note: a kiln is an oven for drying things like hops or timber

indicators.note: a letter placed in a word goes inside it
in disarray means in a mess, so the letters of the back word are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: Something sealed that keeps out moisture, with a judge's rear end in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The judge's letter sits inside the shuffled back word. A Kilner jar is a British brand of glass preserving jar.
explanation.definitionFit: A Kilner jar is a glass preserving jar with a rubber seal, so its whole purpose is to be airtight.

clue.text: Column that's fresh verges on exceptional

parts.note: fresh means new

indicators.note: verges are the edges, so only the outside letters of the next word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A newspaper column that's fresh borders on brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' suggests a newspaper feature; it is an architectural post.
explanation.definitionFit: A newel is the central column of a spiral staircase, or the post at the foot of a banister.

clue.text: Return of former period — les lèche-vitrines love this display

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: late means former, as in 'the late president'
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: The comeback of a past era, which French window-shoppers adore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lèche-vitrines' is French for window-shopping (literally window-licking), so its devotees love a shop display.
explanation.definitionFit: Étalage is the French word, used in English, for a display of goods in a shop window.
